title: Container With Most Water
directAnswer: Maximize area = (distance between two lines) × (height of the shorter line). The interview-grade answer is two pointers starting at both ends: compute the area, then move the pointer at the shorter wall inward — moving the taller one can never help. O(n) time, O(1) space, beating the O(n²) all-pairs brute force.

remember.pattern: Two pointers from both ends, move the shorter wall
remember.formula:
l, r = 0, n-1
best = 0
while l < r:
    area = (r - l) * min(h[l], h[r])
    best = max(best, area)
    if h[l] < h[r]: l += 1
    else: r -= 1
return best
rules: Area is bounded by the **shorter** of the two walls × the width between them.
Always move the pointer at the **shorter** wall — moving the taller one can only shrink or tie the area.
Start as wide as possible (both ends); width only decreases, so you trade width for a chance at more height.
On a tie (`h[l] == h[r]`), moving either is fine — the area can't improve by keeping both.
This is **not** the same as trapping rain water — here you pick exactly two lines, not sum trapped water.
whenToUse: Maximize/minimize a quantity defined by a pair of endpoints
The metric depends on width and the min/max of two endpoint values
You can argue one pointer is always safe to move (a greedy exchange argument)
Brute force is all-pairs O(n²) and you want O(n)
antiSignals: You must sum a contribution across all positions → that's Trapping Rain Water, not this
The pair must satisfy a sum/target rather than maximize area → Two Sum family
Order of elements can change → sorting problems, not fixed-position lines
remember.takeaway: When a quantity depends on two endpoints and the binding constraint is the smaller one, two pointers with a 'move the limiting side' rule finds the optimum in one pass. The proof that discarding the shorter wall loses nothing is the insight interviewers want to hear.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you can prove that moving the shorter wall is always safe and turn an O(n²) pair search into an O(n) two-pointer sweep with a greedy exchange argument.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Moving the taller wall (or both), or confusing this with trapping rain water and trying to sum water over every index.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State brute force, then justify the two-pointer move out loud: 'the area is capped by the shorter wall, so keeping it can never beat moving it — therefore discard it.' That correctness argument is the whole point.

problemStatement:
You are given an integer array `height` of length `n`. There are `n` vertical lines drawn such that the two endpoints of the `iᵗʰ` line are `(i, 0)` and `(i, height[i])`.

Find two lines that together with the x-axis form a container, such that the container contains the **most water**. Return the maximum amount of water a container can store.

Notice that you may not slant the container.
understanding: Pick two of the vertical lines. The water they hold is the rectangle between them: its width is the index distance, its height is the shorter of the two lines (water spills over the lower wall). Maximize that rectangle's area. We choose two lines only — the bars between them are irrelevant here.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the container's height the taller or shorter wall?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: The shorter wall — water above it would spill over the lower side, so min(height[l], height[r]) caps it.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do the lines between the two chosen ones matter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Unlike trapping rain water, we pick exactly two lines and the bars between them are ignored.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can heights be zero?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. A zero-height wall gives zero area for any pair that uses it.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I return the area or the pair of indices?

approaches.name: Brute Force — Check Every Pair
approaches.whenToMention: Say it first to anchor the O(n²) baseline and to motivate the greedy two-pointer move.
hints: The most direct reading: the answer is some pair of lines. How many pairs are there?
Try every pair (i, j) with i < j. The area is (j - i) * min(height[i], height[j]).
Track the maximum across all pairs. It's correct but quadratic — your cue to find structure that lets you skip pairs.
approaches.complexityReasoning: C(n,2) ≈ n²/2 pairs, each evaluated in O(1). No extra storage beyond the running maximum → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Consider every unordered pair of lines `(i, j)` and compute the rectangle they enclose: width `j - i` times the shorter height `min(height[i], height[j])`. Keep the largest area seen.

**Why this is the natural first attempt.** The answer is literally 'the best pair of lines', so enumerating all pairs is the obvious correct baseline. Stating it shows you understand the area formula before optimizing.

**Why we don't ship this.** With `n` up to `10⁵`, n²/2 is about 5 billion pairs — far too slow. The inefficiency is that we re-examine pairs that can't possibly beat what we've found. The two-pointer method exploits a property that lets us discard a whole wall at a time instead of one pair at a time.
approaches.insight: Brute force treats all pairs as equally worth checking. The key observation it misses: starting from the widest pair and shrinking, the *only* way a narrower container can beat a wider one is by being taller — so the shorter wall is the thing holding us back, and it's safe to abandon it.

pitfalls: Using max instead of min for the height — water can't sit higher than the shorter wall.
Off-by-one on width (using j - i + 1) — the container width is the index distance j - i.

approaches.name: Two Pointers — Move the Shorter Wall (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Lead with the correctness argument, not just 'use two pointers'.
hints: Start with the widest possible container — one pointer at each end. Any other container is narrower, so to beat this you need more height.
The area is capped by the shorter wall. If you move the taller wall inward, width shrinks and the height is still capped by that same shorter wall — area can't grow.
So always move the pointer at the shorter wall. That's the only move that could expose a taller wall and possibly increase the area.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each step moves one pointer inward and they never move apart, so the pointers meet after at most n steps → O(n) time. Only two indices and a running max are stored → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
Place `l` at index 0 and `r` at index `n-1` — the widest container possible. Compute its area, update the best, then advance the pointer sitting at the *shorter* wall. Repeat until the pointers meet.

**Why starting widest is the right frame.** Width is maximal at the ends and can only shrink as pointers move inward. So every future container is narrower; the only thing that can make a narrower container win is a taller limiting wall. That reframes the search from 'try all pairs' to 'try to find a taller wall before width costs too much.'

**Why moving the shorter wall is provably safe — the exchange argument.** Suppose `height[l] < height[r]`. The current area is `(r − l) × height[l]`. Consider keeping `l` fixed and moving `r` to any `r' < r`. The width `r' − l` is strictly smaller, and the height is still at most `height[l]` (the shorter wall, unchanged). So *every* container that keeps the short wall `l` is no better than the one we just measured. We can therefore discard `l` forever and move it inward — we lose nothing, and only by doing so might we find a wall taller than `height[l]`. The symmetric argument holds when the right wall is shorter.

**Why this finds the global optimum.** Each pointer move permanently eliminates one wall as a left/right endpoint, but only after we've recorded the best container that wall could ever participate in. Since no discarded option could have beaten what we measured, the maximum we track is the true maximum.

**Why O(1) space and one pass.** Two indices and a running maximum — nothing scales with input size, and each element is passed at most once.
approaches.insight: The whole algorithm rests on one exchange argument: the shorter wall caps the area, and any container still using that shorter wall is narrower and therefore no better — so abandon it. Spotting which endpoint is 'safe to discard' is the transferable skill; it turns many O(n²) pair searches into O(n) sweeps.

pitfalls: Moving the taller wall — width shrinks while the cap stays the same, so you can miss the optimum.
Recomputing with max instead of min for height.
Confusing this with Trapping Rain Water and trying to accumulate water over every index.

commonMistakes: Moving the taller wall instead of the shorter one.
Using max(height[l], height[r]) — the container can't hold water above the shorter wall.
Mixing this up with Trapping Rain Water (summing trapped water vs choosing two lines).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Moving the wrong (taller) wall
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If the right wall is taller and you move it, width shrinks but the height is still capped by the unchanged shorter left wall — you can only lose area and may skip the optimum.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Using max instead of min for the height
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Water spills over the lower wall, so the usable height is the shorter of the two lines, not the taller.

patternNote: Two pointers with a greedy 'move the limiting endpoint' rule. Reach for it when a value depends on two endpoints and you can prove one side is always safe to discard. Cousin of Trapping Rain Water and 3Sum.
